{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q021_nad_binding_convergent_evolution","answer":"SCOPe 2.08 shows that NAD(P) use is not a single evolutionary lineage. It occurs in distinct folds, including the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann fold c.2, FAD/NAD(P)-binding fold c.3, DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding fold c.31, ferredoxin-like HMG-CoA-reductase NAD-binding superfamily d.58.20, and NAD-kinase-like fold e.52. Similar dinucleotide binding in these different global topologies is therefore best treated as convergent—or at least as lacking demonstrated common ancestry—because the chemistry and shape of NAD/NADP impose similar binding constraints. A fold assignment itself describes topology, not homology, and even shared class c merely denotes broad alpha/beta architecture.

Divergence is supported at a different hierarchical level. Within the c.2.1 Rossmann superfamily, SCOPe places distinct families such as alcohol-dehydrogenase-like c.2.1.1, tyrosine-dependent oxidoreductases c.2.1.2, GAPDH-like c.2.1.3, and formate/glycerate-dehydrogenase NAD domains c.2.1.4. Superfamily membership supports probable remote common ancestry followed by divergence; family membership is stronger, generally closer evolutionary evidence. Neither level guarantees identical reaction or substrate specificity.

Cofactor binding alone is unsafe evidence of homology because NAD(P) is ubiquitous and its adenine, ribose, pyrophosphate, and nicotinamide groups favor recurrent local geometries and short motifs. Likewise, similar catalytic residues can arise by chemical constraint, and a locally similar active site need not imply similarity across the rest of the domain. Such observations cannot by themselves distinguish convergence from conserved ancestry, establish NAD versus NADP preference, or justify transferring substrate, reaction, mechanism, stereospecificity, or biological role.

A homology claim instead needs independent, domain-wide evidence: significant sequence similarity with adequate coverage, correspondence of global topology and domain boundaries, structural alignment beyond the binding pocket, conserved residues in homologous positions, and coherent phylogenetic evidence. Biochemical evidence is required for detailed function transfer. For template or representative selection, cofactor identity or a local-site match is insufficient: prefer a same-family representative with compatible full-domain architecture and boundaries plus verified ligand/reaction annotation; a same-superfamily template may support remote structural modeling but only cautious functional inference, while a fold-only match is not a homology-based functional template.","evidence_used":["mcp__scope__get_scop_service_info — /api/v1/, /api/v1/releases/current","mcp__scope__search_scop — /api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=NAD&mode=token&limit=50","mcp__scope__get_scop_node — /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2/parents, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.3, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.3/parents, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.31, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.31/parents, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.58.20, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/d.58.20/parents, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/e.52, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/e.52/parents, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1, /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1/parents","mcp__scope__list_scop_children — /api/v1/releases/2.08/sccs/c.2.1/children?limit=50"]}]}
